clue.text: Holding on to notes, stout ones collapse

indicators.note: when the two words collapse they fall into a heap and are rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: A drinker's bottles of stout fall over while someone holds a long musical note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collapse' tells you to rearrange STOUT and ONES together; the result is the musical direction for sustaining notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sostenuto is the Italian performance marking telling a player to sustain each sound.

clue.text: Tube so confoundedly dull …

indicators.note: confounded means thrown into confusion, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that the London Underground is maddeningly boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confoundedly' reads as a mild oath but tells you to rearrange TUBE and SO. The Tube is London's Underground railway.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtuse describes someone slow-witted, a synonym of dull in the sense of not sharp.

clue.text: … not the practice of the Circle Line

parts.note: a circle is drawn as the round letter O
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue: the London Underground's Circle Line works only on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to the Tube clue, so 'Circle Line' looks like the London Underground route; it is split into O and RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Theory and practice are the standard pair of opposites, so what is not practice is abstract principle.

clue.text: Bother! It induces a rash

definitions.meaning: to bother someone is to irritate or annoy them, a verb
a stinging plant whose touch brings the skin out in itchy bumps

explanation.surface: Someone curses as they brush against a plant and break out in spots.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to irk or annoy, and the stinging weed of that name raises a rash on the skin.

clue.text: Things wrong with common noses expert directors needed

parts.note: troubles are things that have gone wrong
hooters is a slang, common, word for noses

explanation.surface: A firm with problems and a pack of nosy busybodies needs skilled managers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'common' means vulgar or slang here, not ordinary: HOOTERS is slang for noses.
explanation.definitionFit: Troubleshooters are specialists brought in to direct the fixing of problems in an organisation.

clue.text: Feature of the Oval, cut used more

parts.note: a gash is a deep cut
something used more is older, more worn

explanation.surface: A remark about the cricket ground, its turf slashed and worn by heavy use.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oval is a London cricket ground famous for the huge Victorian gas-storage tanks that overlook it.
explanation.definitionFit: The great iron gas-storage tanks beside the Oval are a well-known landmark of that ground.

clue.text: Namely, vindicator of the garbage-disposer

parts.note: SC abbreviates Latin scilicet, meaning namely
a vindicator who exacts retribution is an avenger

explanation.surface: Someone names the champion who stands up for the rubbish collector.
explanation.walkthrough: SC, short for scilicet, is a dictionary abbreviation for 'namely'; 'of the' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A scavenger feeds on refuse and carrion, clearing away waste.

clue.text: Twinkler peach, it grows in the tropics

parts.note: a star twinkles in the night sky
to peach is old slang for inform on someone, as is to grass

explanation.surface: A sparkling peach is described as a fruit of hot climates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peach' looks like the fruit but is the verb meaning to inform on someone, which is also to grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Stargrass is a name for several tropical plants with star-shaped flowers.

clue.text: Thousand on racecourse is held to be lucky

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
Ascot is a famous English racecourse

explanation.surface: A punter's thousand-pound bet at the races is thought to be a good omen.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a racecourse in Berkshire, England, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: A mascot is a person, animal or object believed to bring good fortune.

clue.text: Heed the word of a drill sergeant

definitions.meaning: notice or care paid to something, a noun

definitions.text: the word of a drill sergeant
definitions.meaning: the command shouted to make soldiers stand straight

explanation.surface: A recruit is told to listen to what the sergeant barks on the parade ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Heed means notice taken, and the parade-ground command calling troops to stand stiffly upright is that same word.

clue.text: Barely a youngster, he does not need one yet

definitions.text: Barely a youngster, he does not need one yet

parts.words: Barely a youngster, he does not need one yet
parts.note: a young lad is called a young ..., and a boy with a smooth chin has no use for an electric razor

explanation.surface: A boy so young his face is bare has no need yet of a razor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'young shaver' is an old phrase for a lad; the same word is the electric razor he does not yet need, and 'Barely' plays on his bare chin.
explanation.definitionFit: A shaver is both a boy and an electric razor, and the clue uses both senses.

clue.text: Refined basalt ore used by old astronomers

indicators.note: refining ore reworks it, so these letters are processed into a new order

explanation.surface: Smelted volcanic rock and ore are put to use by early stargazers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refined' signals an anagram of BASALT and ORE; the definition describes the instrument by its users.
explanation.definitionFit: An astrolabe was the instrument early astronomers used to measure the altitude of stars.

clue.text: Aircraft at top of first runway is smoother

indicators.note: the aircraft sits at the head, so its letters come before the following piece

parts.note: a plane is an aircraft

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the next word, runway

explanation.surface: A plane positioned at the start of the main runway is quieter on take-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smoother' is not a comparative adjective but a noun, a tool that smooths: PLANE followed by R.
explanation.definitionFit: A planer is a woodworking tool that shaves a surface flat, so it is one that smooths.

clue.text: Prove a tea, stirred, will disappear into thin air

indicators.note: stirring mixes things up, so these letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A tea, once stirred, is shown to vanish into the air as steam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirred' tells you to rearrange PROVE A TEA; 'will' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: To evaporate is to turn to vapour and vanish, as in vanishing without trace.

clue.text: Policy women tend to con V vert

indicators.note: to convert something is to change it into another form, here a new order of letters

explanation.surface: Women tend to be persuaded by a sales pitch for an insurance plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Policy' looks like a political programme but is an insurance product; 'to convert' is the anagram signal, changing the form of the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An endowment is a type of life-insurance policy paying out at a fixed date.

clue.text: Guard a long way off, dismissed, sent by rail

parts.note: a batter who is dismissed in cricket is out
taken as written
RY is the abbreviation for railway, the rail network

explanation.surface: A distant sentry, sacked, is shipped home by train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is link; out-sentry is an old military term for a guard posted beyond the lines.
explanation.definitionFit: An out-sentry is a soldier posted on watch at a distance ahead of the main body.

clue.text: It is dry in wine-house cellars

indicators.note: in tells you the answer is tucked inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A dry wine is kept down in the tavern's cellar.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of 'wine-house' and 'cellars'; 'It is' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: Sec is the French wine term for not sweet.

clue.text: Could be overcast in three directions

parts.note: south is a compass direction, abbreviated S
east is a second compass direction, abbreviated E
west is a third compass direction, abbreviated W

explanation.surface: A forecaster says the sky may be cloudy in several parts of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overcast' looks like a weather word, but it is also a sewing stitch over an edge; 'in' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: Overcasting is a stitch whipped over a raw edge, so an overcast seam is stitched.

clue.text: Expression of surprise, following the bill?

definitions.meaning: an exclamation like 'well I never!', a British interjection
doves are said to bill and ..., so the soft call follows the billing

explanation.surface: Someone gasps on seeing the restaurant bill.
explanation.walkthrough: The bill looks like a restaurant charge; it is a bird's beak, from the phrase 'bill and coo' for courting doves.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a British exclamation of astonishment and the soft call doves make after touching beaks.

clue.text: Derring-do, taking risks on loch-monster's SE venue, possibly

indicators.note: possibly says these letters might make something else if reordered

parts.note: the word monster with its S kept as a letter

explanation.surface: Daring adventurers hunt the creature at its home in Loch Ness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals an anagram of MONSTERS, SE and VENUE; the S of the possessive is needed as a letter. The surface points to the Loch Ness monster.
explanation.definitionFit: Venturesomeness is boldness and willingness to take chances, the same quality as daring exploits.

clue.text: Doctor one sees at home?

parts.note: a doctor met in the living room rather than the surgery is the time-travelling one on the family TV

explanation.surface: A patient asks which doctor makes house calls.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a GP's home visit, but the doctor is the long-running BBC science-fiction hero watched on television at home.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC Time Lord is known only as the Doctor, and the show's title asks his name.

clue.text: French writer coming out of stupor

indicators.note: coming out of a stupor, the word is roused and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A novelist wakes from a daze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming out of' looks like extraction, but all six letters of STUPOR are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust wrote the novel sequence In Search of Lost Time.

clue.text: Rue des Anglais?

parts.note: read as French, a street of the English; read with the English verb, the sorrowful sense of rue

explanation.surface: A street name in a French town, honouring the English.
explanation.walkthrough: In French 'rue' is a street, but in English 'rue' means to feel sorry; 'des Anglais' asks for the English meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue an act is to wish it undone, the English sense of the word.

clue.text: Does he issue bank statements?

parts.note: a cashier at a bank counter, and also one who tells or makes statements

explanation.surface: A customer asks whether a bank clerk sends out account summaries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bank statements' suggests account printouts; the person is a bank cashier, whose job title also means one who tells, makes statements.
explanation.definitionFit: A teller is a bank cashier and, literally, one who tells, gives statements.

clue.text: Science master has a bad. reputation

definitions.meaning: school slang for a chemistry teacher
is held in low regard, a verb phrase

explanation.surface: A school's chemistry teacher is unpopular.
explanation.walkthrough: British public-school slang called chemistry, and its master, by this name, from the smells of the lab. The stray full stop is a print flaw.
explanation.definitionFit: Old British school slang names chemistry and its teacher after lab smells, and the verb means is thought very poor.

clue.text: Piano piece from a short story

definitions.meaning: a short romantic piano composition, as in Schumann's set
a brief, often sentimental work of fiction

explanation.surface: A pianist's party piece is taken from a brief tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from a' is link between the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a short lyrical keyboard work, made famous by Schumann, and a short romantic novel.

clue.text: Jog, tear round the first motorway

indicators.note: round means the word for tear goes around the other piece

parts.note: to rend is to tear
the M1 was Britain's first motorway, read as the letters M and I

explanation.surface: A jogger tears around the opening stretch of motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jog' is the verb as in jog the memory; the M1, London to Leeds, was Britain's first full motorway.
explanation.definitionFit: To jog someone's memory is to prompt it, which is what reminding does.

clue.text: Courage set down in vitally important part of country

parts.note: heart means courage, as in take heart
to land is to set down, as an aircraft does

explanation.surface: Bravery is laid down in the core region of a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is link.
explanation.definitionFit: A heartland is the central region of a country, on which it depends most.

clue.text: Occupation of railwaymen in driving situation

indicators.note: in means the union is placed inside the golf term

parts.note: in golf you drive off from the tee
NUR is the National Union of Railwaymen, a former British trade union

explanation.surface: Train drivers have a job in the driving seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'driving situation' suggests a train cab but means a golf tee, where you drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Tenure is the holding or occupying of an office or property.

clue.text: Order tries some, keeping secrets

indicators.note: order as a verb means arrange, so these letters are put into a new sequence

explanation.surface: A secret religious order puts some initiates through tests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' reads as a religious order but tells you to rearrange TRIES and SOME.
explanation.definitionFit: Esoterism is the practice of keeping teaching hidden, available only to initiates.
